text: ﻿The history of speech synthesis is a long and surprisingly stubborn one.

For most of the twentieth century, the best a machine could do was imitate a human voice in the crudest possible way, buzzing through a bank of analog filters and hoping the listener would fill in the gaps.
The results were intelligible, barely, and they sounded like a robot trapped inside a pipe.
Then came concatenative synthesis, which stitched together thousands of tiny recorded fragments, and for a while that was good enough for telephone menus and talking clocks.
Neural networks changed the rules entirely.

Instead of assembling pieces of recorded speech, a network could learn the mapping from text to waveform directly, and by the early twenty twenties the best systems were nearly indistinguishable from a person reading aloud.
The catch was size.
A good neural voice often needed hundreds of millions of parameters, a GPU, and a small power station to run in real time.
Paradee takes the opposite bet.
It asks how small a voice can be before it stops being useful, and it answers with fewer than eight million parameters, a single eight megabyte file, and a decoder that never upsamples.
The result is a model that speaks faster than you can listen, on one thread of an ordinary laptop processor, with no graphics card and no network connection.
That is the whole point.
A voice that runs anywhere is a voice that can live inside a browser tab, a phone, a cheap embedded board, or a program you wrote on a rainy afternoon.
It will not win a contest against a giant model trained on a thousand hours of studio recordings, but it does not need to.
It needs to be small, fast, and clear, and on all three counts it delivers.
The old lighthouse keeper climbed the spiral stairs every evening at dusk.
She counted the steps out of habit, though she no longer needed to.
Forty-two steps, then a landing, then thirty more to the lamp room.
The storm had knocked out the power three days ago, and the backup generator was failing.
Outside, waves hammered the rocks with a rhythm that never quite repeated.
He asked her once why she stayed, and she said the light was a promise.
On the mainland, people forgot the lighthouse existed until the night it went dark.
A fishing boat ran aground on the northern shoal, and the crew of four survived.
After that, the town council voted to fund a full-time keeper again.
She took the job without hesitation, though her doctor advised against it.
The salary was modest, but the view from the lamp room was worth more than money.
Every night at sunset, she lit the lamp and swept the glass until it gleamed.
Children from the village sometimes visited on weekends, asking endless questions.
One boy wanted to know if she was ever afraid, and she laughed.
Fear, she said, is just respect for something bigger than yourself.
The sea taught her that lesson decades ago, and she never forgot it.
Modern navigation systems had made lighthouses obsolete, everyone told her.
Yet ships still passed close on foggy nights, watching for her beam.
Technology fails, she replied, but a steady light never does.
When she finally retired at seventy, the village threw her a party.
The new keeper was a young man from the city who had never seen the ocean.
She spent a week teaching him the routines, the maintenance, the patience.
On her last night, she climbed the stairs one final time and lit the lamp.
Then she sat in the doorway and watched the sun rise over the water.
It was, she later wrote in her journal, a good ending to a good story.

"Are you coming?" she asked from the hallway.
"In a minute," he called back, still tying his shoes.
"We are going to be late," she warned, tapping her foot.
"I am ready now," he said, grabbing his coat.
"Finally," she said with a smile, and they left together.
"What did the doctor say?" he asked quietly.
"It is nothing serious," she replied, though she looked worried.
"Do you want me to come with you?" he offered.
"No, I can manage," she said, but her voice shook slightly.
"Call me the moment you hear anything," he insisted.
"I will," she promised, and she meant it.
"How long have we known each other?" she asked suddenly.
"Fifteen years, give or take," he answered without hesitation.
"It feels longer," she said, laughing softly.
"That is because you have a bad memory," he teased.
"Maybe," she admitted, "but you love me anyway."
"That I do," he said, and he closed the door behind them.
"Where should we eat?" she asked as they walked.
"Anywhere without a wait," he said, and they both laughed.
"Deal," she said, and they turned the corner together.
